p:IRN: The Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran issues the rial, which is in free fall. Its law leaves most power with government, 0.448 of 1 where 1 means the bank holds it. Its notes and coins come from the Security Printing and Minting Organization, a state printing works owned by the bank since 1962; before 1982 the notes were printed abroad. The governor appointed in August 2013 came in from private banking, which is a career move and not an accusation: the bank's general assembly appointed Valiollah Seif, described in local press as having been managing director of the privately owned Karafarin Bank, in place of Mahmud Bahmani, and that report is what states the employer's private ownership. The government then replaced Seif on 25 July 2018 with no reason given, and dismissed his successor Abdolnasser Hemmati on 30 May 2021 because he was standing in the 18 June presidential election, naming deputy Akbar Komijani in his place. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced Seif to ten years in prison, his former deputy Araghchi to eight and the intermediary Salar Aghakhani to thirteen over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018, in which the judiciary said ten people were identified; the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, citing insufficient evidence and authorisation by higher authorities, and the judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025. Abroad, Bahrain's High Criminal Court in November 2020 fined the bank and other Iran-owned banks, including Future Bank, one million Bahraini dinars each and jailed three Future Bank officials for five years; prosecutors said the Central Bank of Iran planned to launder billions of dollars through Future Bank, which handled suspicious transfers favouring Iranian entities without reporting them. Bahrain's top court upheld the conviction in 2021, with five Future Bank officials given ten-year sentences and a sixth five years, and confiscation of remittances estimated at 184 million US dollars, 967 million euros, 53 million dirhams and 235 billion Iranian riyals. Iran scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, 24th of 194.
p:NIC: Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than market value and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is described as 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. Two career moves are recorded, and a career move is not an accusation. Luis Rivas Anduray was an economic adviser at the bank from 2001 to 2002, ran the finance ministry's fiscal affairs office from 2002 to 2003, and became general manager of Banpro at the end of 2004, where he is now chief executive and a director; Banpro's majority shareholder is Grupo Promerica, of Panamanian origin, described as the second Central American financial group of private capital, and Banpro was owned by the Nicaraguan businessman Ramiro Ortiz Mayorga, which is how that employer's private ownership is established. The man who now runs the bank came to it from the government: Ovidio Reyes was Chief Economist at the Ministry of Finance from 2004 to 2012, became the bank's General Manager in 2012-13 and its President in January 2014, a move between two public bodies, with no private employer named. At the end of 2024 the statute governing the bank was rewritten in a week. The presidency sent the National Assembly the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero on 19 December 2024; it went to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, was approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. It repealed the bank's own organic law and the law governing the Superintendency of Banks and Other Financial Institutions, and put the two institutions, until then independent of each other, under one statute and one common board chaired by Reyes, abolishing the Superintendency's own board; Reyes was also given coordination of the Financial Analysis Unit and the deposit fund. The law's own text says the institutions keep organic, functional, administrative, financial and budgetary autonomy and their institutional specialisation. Divergentes read it the other way, writing that the law eliminates the autonomy of the monetary and financial institutions and gives plenipotentiary powers to Reyes and to the Executive, and that removing the cross-checks between supervisor and central bank removes a safeguard against political and economic bias. Article 24 obliges every person resident or domiciled in Nicaragua, national or foreign, to give the bank and the Superintendency whatever economic, financial, statistical and regulatory information they ask for. The bank did not object publicly and its president gained authority rather than losing it; what changed was that the law governing the bank was rewritten by the Executive, without consultation. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.
p:ABW: The Central Bank of Aruba, created in 1986, issues the Aruban florin and holds it at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its Central Bank Ordinance of 1991, amended through 2014, keeps the bank under the Governor of Aruba and the Minister of Finance. Section 18 has the Governor appoint the president and executive directors from a shortlist of three put up by the Supervisory Board, and suspend or dismiss them by state decree; section 19(3) allows general guidelines for their duties to be set by decree; section 23 gives him the appointment and dismissal of the supervisory directors; and section 27(1) has the Government Commissioner supervise the bank under the Minister's instructions. This is a standing arrangement with no end date. One case is recorded: the General Audit Chamber, reviewing the country's 2001-2004 accounts, found contributions paid into an earmarked account at the bank for the Fondo Desaroyo Aruba foundation were not accounted for completely, correctly and on time, with 16,898,503 florins paid in by the Netherlands left off the balance sheet out of a 19.3 million florin balance at the end of 2000. The president who held the post until the end of 2025 spent her working life in public bodies: Jeanette R. (Jane) Semeleer began as a management adviser at Aruba's Department of Economic Affairs, later worked at the Department of External Relations, joined the bank in 1990, was appointed Executive Director in 2000 and President in 2008, and retired on 1 December 2025; no private employer is named. Her successor arrives from commercial banking, which is a career move and not an accusation: Thomas Domhoff takes up the presidency on 1 July 2026, and his career, as reported on 1 April 2026, covers work on major projects at ING, ABN AMRO, Rabobank and Capgemini, a directorship at Banco Sicredi, a chief executive post at Castrolanda Agroindustrial and the restructuring of Girobank's legacy portfolio through GI-RO Settlement Holding; ING's own largest-investors page states that ING Group is a publicly-listed company and names BlackRock, which disclosed 7.3 per cent of its issued share capital, and Amundi Asset Management among holders above 3 per cent, which is how that employer's private ownership is established. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied new banknotes in 2019, on a client list in another organisation's announcement rather than a contract notice, so that is reported rather than confirmed by the bank. BNP Paribas Asset Management runs a fixed income mandate in US dollars and gives advice, and Ernst & Young audits the accounts. Aruba scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:COD: The Central Bank of the Congo issues the country's money. In April 2021 a report by Congo's state finance inspectorate, the IGF, called a 43 million US dollar transfer from a central bank account at BGFI Bank to the food importer Egal an embezzlement of public funds, and said the bank kept false accounts to cover it: its 2013 accounts showed about 43.1 million dollars in that account when the real balance was about 119,000 dollars. The former governor Deogratias Mutombo, the bank and PricewaterhouseCoopers did not respond to the journalists who reported this from leaked BGFI documents. On 25 October 2023 the accounts of Mutombo and of Albert Yuma, former board chairman of the mining company Gecamines, were frozen over an alleged embezzlement of 25.521 million dollars, with both men required to remain available to the national audit court; that allegation is unproven and still under investigation. Belgium's federal prosecutor also opened a money laundering investigation into Mutombo and five others over hundreds of thousands of dollars allegedly moved through Belgium, with searches in September 2023; as of October 2024 the prosecutor said no suspect had been charged. A career move out of the bank is also recorded, and it is not an accusation: Leny Ilondo's career at the bank included the position of Director before he retired, and he joined the board of Rawbank in 2024 as a non-executive director sitting on its risk and audit committees; the only description of who owns Rawbank is its own annual report's chairman's letter, which calls the shareholding family and entrepreneurial, names no individual shareholders and does not call it a private commercial bank. The bank scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Giesecke+Devrient printed the 200-franc note issued on 31 July 2007, and its imprint on the 100-franc note is the only record of who printed that one. The bank's accounts are audited by Ernst & Young RDC of Kinshasa for 2024. In a communique that reached the state news agency ACP on Wednesday 23 September 2026 the Cour des comptes, Congo's audit court, announced an audit mission at the Central Bank of the Congo to examine the bank's treasury operations for the 2025 financial year, as part of checking how the 2025 finance law was carried out. The court's First President, Jimmy Munganga, instructed the bank's services to hand the auditors the documents they need. No start or end date is given, and parliament's review of the 2025 accounts-settlement bill and of the 2027 finance bill waits on the court filing its report.
p:IRQ: The Central Bank of Iraq issues the dinar and keeps it within a band of 2 percent or less against the US dollar. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 0.733 of 1 for the independence written into its law, where 1 means the bank holds the power and 0 the government. In 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit examined the bank's daily auctions of dollars to banks and found that most transactions rested on fraudulent paperwork; the country's top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally, as reported by the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi and named a successor while a parliamentary committee was examining possible manipulation of the dinar and charging that bank officials were abusing the dollar sales. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without saying what the charges were. The integrity committee's chairman said the inquiry was not about money but about procedures, while a member of the finance committee called it a political decision and not professional; al-Shabibi's defence called the case politically motivated. No court outcome was ever found, so nothing was proven; he died on 8 January 2022, and the bank mourned him as a distinguished former governor. One career move is on record, and it stays inside the public sector: on 14 March 2023 the governor appointed Faisal Wisam al-Heims as deputy governor, from the post of Director-General of the Trade Bank of Iraq, which the report describes as a state-owned bank, and he had also chaired the Iraq Securities Commission, a regulator, so neither side of the move is private finance. It holds 175.6 tonnes of gold, and the Board of Supreme Audit audits its accounts. Who prints the dinar rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than anything the bank publishes: it says the 2003 series, still the basis of circulating notes, was printed by De La Rue.
p:LSO: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho, replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and then by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined; member currencies are pegged to the rand at par and are legal tender only in the country that issues them, Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there as legal tender. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. One career move is recorded, and it is not an accusation: Mr. O. 'Nete, a non-executive director on the bank's board, came from Standard Bank of Lesotho, where he was Senior Finance Manager, Finance Manager and Senior Manager Personal Credit, and earlier from Stanlib, where he was Tax Manager, with no dates given; Standard Bank Group's own structure page lists Standard Lesotho Bank Limited at 80 per cent among its holdings as at 30 June 2026, so that employer is majority owned by the Johannesburg-listed group rather than by the state. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60. At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, the parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. Its chairperson, 'Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures in the report do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the consolidated accounts, a difference of M3.09 billion, which a quotation in the same piece also gives. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget for the audit by 30 June so it could go into the supplementary budget; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for one. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes for the state.
p:GUY: The Bank of Guyana issues the Guyanese dollar, held at what is in practice a fixed rate to the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 56, with the country scoring 40 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. Part of the bank's work is handed to ministers by the law itself, and that is a standing arrangement rather than a passing dispute: under section 29 of the Bank of Guyana Act, Chapter 85:02 (Act No. 19 of 1998, enacted 31 December 1998), the Minister, in consultation with the Bank, specifies the policies, principles and criteria of Guyana's exchange rate system, and the Bank is responsible only for the day-to-day administration of that system; section 14(2) lets the President terminate the appointment of the Governor, and the Minister terminate the appointment of any other Director, on stated grounds; section 3(1) describes the Bank as an autonomous institution governed by the Act. Independence written into its law scores 0.609 of 1, ranking 93 of 191, and no government pressure was reported in 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded, and it ended in an official finding. The Auditor General, Deodat Sharma, reported in his 2013 report that eight accounts at the Bank of Guyana holding about 1.8 billion Guyana dollars had sat unused for more than five years, untouched since 2009: 474 million for UK Programme Aid-GEA, 371 million for the Infrastructural Development Fund, 280 million for the Agriculture Rehabilitation Project, 213 million for SIMAP Phase II, 172 million for the Financial Sector Reform Programme, 127 million for Accountant General-GEC Wartsila, 77 million for an Agriculture Loan and 55 million for UK Programme Aid-Rice. His Audit Office had reviewed eleven special accounts at the bank with balances of about 4.3 billion dollars in total; he said the money belonged in the Consolidated Fund and recommended the Ministry of Finance transfer it there as soon as possible, noting that on that basis the government's overall bank position would show a positive balance of 56 billion dollars. Two career moves are on record. The first is entirely within the public sector, so it is listed but not counted: governor Gobind Ganga directed the bank's research department from 1995 to November 2003, left to be an alternate executive director at the World Bank in Washington, returned as deputy governor in June 2005 and became governor on 2 December 2014, his earlier posts being academic, with no private employer anywhere in the career the bank publishes. The second runs the other way and into private banking: Demerara Bank Limited, which its own audited accounts describe as incorporated on 20 January 1992 as a private limited liability company, publishes a profile of its director Rajendra Rampersaud saying he has over two decades of central banking experience and served as a Director at the Bank of Guyana until 2018. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied banknotes, banknote paper and anti-counterfeiting features, though that comes from a client list in another body's announcement rather than a contract notice. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:CAN: The Bank of Canada issues the Canadian dollar, which moves within a band of 2% or less against the US dollar. Canada scores 23 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; that is 179th of 194, less exposed than 92 percent of the places with a figure. One case is documented, and it ended in an official finding: two internal audits of the bank from 2004, released under the Access to Information Act, one of them dated 15 October, criticised it for slack financial practices, finding that employees paid invoices without authorization, did not evaluate whether they got good value from suppliers, and violated a fail-safe system meant to guard against cheque fraud. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. Pressure came later and from the opposition rather than the government: at a Conservative leadership debate in Edmonton on 11 May 2022, Pierre Poilievre pledged to fire governor Tiff Macklem if he became prime minister, having called the bank financially illiterate the month before, and also promised to have it audited and to bar it from issuing a digital currency; he repeated the pledge as party leader in December 2022. Macklem had been appointed in 2020 to a seven-year term, and the Bank of Canada Act says the governor is appointed for seven years during good behaviour, so removing one would require Parliament's involvement. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland both defended the bank's independence and former governor David Dodge rejected the criticism; the party's own finance critic, Ed Fast, was removed from that role after saying the pledge was deeply troubling and hurt the party's economic credibility. The bank's own profile of Mark Carney, governor from 1 February 2008 to 1 June 2013, describes a thirteen-year career at the investment bank Goldman Sachs, in its London, Tokyo, New York and Toronto offices, before he entered the public service; he joined the bank as Deputy Governor in August 2003, moved to the Department of Finance in November 2004 and returned as Governor, and no ethics finding is recorded for the move. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Ernst & Young and PricewaterhouseCoopers audit its accounts, Canadian Bank Note Company and BA International print its notes, and Securency International supplies the polymer the notes are made of. The Canadian dollar is 5.76% of world currency trading and 2.47% of foreign reserves, and the bank has 9 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency.
p:CUW: The Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder, pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 95% of the 194 places scored. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts with plants in Malta and Sweden and a supplier to more than 50 central banks, was contracted to print the new banknotes, with the Royal Canadian Mint making the coins. The bank's supervisory board came under pressure in May 2017. A report published on 26 May 2017 said the board had voted three to two to extend a managing director's term, short of the supermajority required, and that the finance minister, Richard Gibson, had written to the board members Robert Pietersz, Tom Kok, Miriela Carolina, Vance Williams and Hubert Lopez asking them to work on a solution; it quotes him saying that if a solution could not be found there would be no other choice but dismissal of the board, without naming who would carry it out. One case is recorded. In July 2024 a court found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over 400,000 dollars went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a 1.5 million dollar payment in 2015 from the Venezuelan company Enpiso, which prosecutors linked to Girobank takeover talks. One career move is documented: Bob Traa became president with effect from 13 June 2019, after working for the International Monetary Fund for over 34 years, and no private employer is named. That was a temporary appointment by the Supervisory Board, pending official appointment by Curacao and Sint Maarten.
p:YEM: The Central Bank of Yemen issues the rial, held close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the corruption and secrecy around it stand at 86. Government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for easier money or for printing money. On 18 September 2016 President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, announcing from Saudi Arabia, sacked central bank head Mohammed bin Hammam, named Mansar al-Kaiti in his place and ordered the bank moved to Aden, with no official reason given. A UN Panel of Experts report in January 2021 said the Aden-based bank broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered 'a substantial part' of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims, and on 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel withdrew the money-laundering and corruption accusations. On 6 December 2021 Hadi dismissed the governor and his deputy, naming Ahmed bin Ahmed Ghaleb Al-Maabq governor and Muhammad Omar Banaja deputy, with no reason given; it was the fourth such sacking since the civil war began. Ernst & Young audits the accounts, a record that rests on the announcement of the appointment on 7 February 2021 and states no financial year. Its money is printed in Russia. The Russian foreign ministry confirmed in June 2020 that the state printer Goznak had been printing notes for Yemen's government under a commercial contract signed in 2017, after separatists in Aden seized a convoy carrying 64 billion rials, about 255 million US dollars, of Russian-printed banknotes.
p:HND: The Central Bank of Honduras issues the lempira, kept as of December 2025 at a set level against the US dollar and moved in small steps, an arrangement called a crawling peg. The man who runs it came from commercial banking, which is a career move and not an accusation: Wilfredo Rafael Cerrato Rodriguez was a credit officer at Banco Mercantil, S.A. from November 1993 to April 1996, a credit officer at Intermediaria Financiera, S.A. of Grupo FICOHSA from September to December 1996, and a credit officer and then agency manager at Banco FICOHSA from January 1997 to February 2003, ten years in Honduran commercial banking before his public career, and he became president of the central bank on 27 January 2018; Banco Ficohsa's audited financial statements state that it is 94.28% owned by Grupo Financiero Ficohsa S.A., domiciled in Panama, which is how the private shareholding of that employer is established, since the biography page itself states no ownership. Its accounts are checked from outside by Horwath Central America, for the 2023 financial year. The 200-lempira note is printed by Crane Currency Malta Limited, which won private tender 11/2023 by resolution 127-3/2024 of 14 March 2024, worth 1,284,000 US dollars at 6.42 US cents a note. One case is documented: on 3 June 2026 prosecutors charged 11 current and former employees, two of them serving managers, with 100 counts of negligent embezzlement over a scheme said to have removed public funds from the bank over several years, and they were arrested after the court admitted the case. The charges are unproven. Honduras scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, the heaviest part being corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 67.
